159.subtitle: Rest for the scorched, proclaimed aloud by the secret texts

commentary.meaning: Three names only, and the first of them occupies the whole of the first line — sixteen syllables of unbroken compound, among the longest single names in the hymn. It says that she gives rest to people scorched by birth, death and old age. After a hundred and fifty verses in which names have come four and six and eight to a verse, the sudden slowing is audible, and it is doing work: the name is long because the condition it describes is long. The second line then makes two claims of a different order. All the Upaniṣads shout her aloud, which is a deliberate paradox given that an upaniṣad is by definition a secret teaching. And she consists of the last of the five phases, the one called Śāntyatītā, which has gone past even stillness. The verse thus moves from the most concrete possible statement of what is wrong with human life to the most abstract term the Śaiva systems possess, in the space of two lines.
commentary.history:
Birth, death and old age form a triad that Indian religious literature returns to so consistently that the compound janma-mṛtyu-jarā functions almost as a single word. The Bhagavadgītā uses it, with sickness added, in its account of what counts as knowledge; the Buddhist formulations of suffering run through the same items; and the medical and ascetic literatures agree on the diagnosis while disagreeing about everything else. The verb inside the compound here is worth noticing: tapta, from √tap, means scorched or burned. The same root gives tapas, the heat generated by ascetic practice, which is a heat one takes on deliberately. Here the heat is not chosen. The people described are being cooked by a process they did not start.

Against that, viśrānti. The word is built on vi plus √śram, to grow weary, and means the cessation of exertion — a rest that comes at the end of effort rather than in the middle of it. It is an ordinary word for a traveller stopping, and it became a technical term of some weight in Kashmiri Śaiva thought, where consciousness coming to rest in itself, rather than chasing outward through its objects, is the whole of what is aimed at. The name does not promise the relief of one difficulty. It promises the end of the exertion, which is why the tradition hears mokṣa in it rather than consolation.

Sarvopaniṣadudghuṣṭā turns on a contradiction that its author clearly enjoyed. Udghuṣṭa is from ud plus √ghuṣ, to shout: it means proclaimed at the top of the voice, cried through the streets, noised abroad. An upaniṣad, on the other hand, is a rahasya, a secret, taught by a teacher sitting with a student and traditionally withheld from anyone unqualified; the classical Advaita derivation of the word takes it from a root sad in the senses of destroying, reaching and loosening, so that the teaching destroys ignorance and loosens the bonds of one who sits near for it. To say that the secret texts shout her aloud is to say that the concealment was never about the subject matter. What is hidden in an Upaniṣad is hidden by the reader's inability, not by the text's reticence.

Whether the Upaniṣads in fact proclaim a goddess is a live question, and the Śākta tradition has answered it by pointing to a small number of passages and by producing more. The classical passage is the episode in the Kena Upaniṣad in which the gods, puffed up by a victory that was not theirs, are confronted by a mysterious presence they cannot identify, and Indra finally learns what it was from a woman who appears in the sky. The Śvetāśvatara's language about a supreme power belonging to the absolute has served the same purpose. Beyond those, the tradition has its own Upaniṣads — the Devī Upaniṣad, the Tripurā and Tripurātāpinī, the Bahvṛca and the Bhāvana — which are late by the standards of the classical texts and openly Śākta in content, and which are what make the claim of "all the Upaniṣads" defensible from inside the tradition even to a reader who thinks it strained from outside.

The last name is technical and rewards precision. Śaiva cosmology divides the whole ladder of reality into five kalās, phases or segments, each covering a band of the thirty-six tattvas. From the bottom they are Nivṛtti, which covers earth alone; Pratiṣṭhā, running from water up through primal nature; Vidyā, covering the soul and the constraints that limit it; Śānti, the pure levels above the fissure between limited and unlimited; and Śāntyatītā, the phase beyond peace, at the top. The scheme is used in initiation, where the officiant purifies the candidate's soul band by band, and in the daily worship of the deity, where the same ladder is climbed in imagination. Two things follow for this verse. First, pratiṣṭhā, which appeared as an independent name only four verses earlier, is a term in the same system, and readers who know the scheme hear the two names as marking the bottom and the top of one ladder. Second, the choice of the highest kalā for a name near the end of the hymn is not accidental: the last portion of the thousand names climbs, and śāntyatītā is deliberately the name of a level for which the word peace is already too positive a description.
commentary.practice:
The first line is a single word of sixteen syllables and it is the chief technical difficulty in this part of the hymn. Do not attempt it as a unit. Break it into its five pieces and learn them separately — janma, mṛtyu, jarā, tapta, jana, then viśrānti and dāyinī — and only then run them together. The junctions that give trouble are jarā-tapta, where a long ā meets a t and the temptation is to shorten the vowel, and tapta-jana, where the p is unreleased before the t.

Mṛtyu contains the vocalic ṛ, a full vowel occupying its own beat, followed immediately by the cluster ty. Say mṛ as one short syllable with the tongue curled, then tyu with the t and y sharing a single release.

Viśrānti has ś, then r, then a long ā, and then the nti cluster; the anusvāra-like nasal before the t is a dental n made where the t is made. Dāyinī ends the line with three open syllables, and the line's whole rhythmic shape depends on arriving at them without having rushed what came before. In performance the line takes as long as a full verse elsewhere in the hymn, and it should.

The second line is easier to say and harder to parse. Sarvopaniṣadudghuṣṭā is sarva plus upaniṣad plus udghuṣṭā, with the a of sarva and the u of upaniṣad combining into o — one of the commonest sandhis in the language, and one worth recognizing on sight, since sarvo- almost always signals it. The cluster dgh in the middle is voiced throughout, d then the aspirated gh, with the aspiration audible as breath and not as a separate syllable. The two ṣ sounds in the word are retroflex and the ṭ in ghuṣṭā is retroflex because of the ṣ before it.

Śāntyatītakalātmikā is śānti plus atīta plus kalā plus ātmikā, and again the joins are all vowel contractions: śānty-atīta, and kalā plus ātmikā giving a single long ā. Say it slowly enough that the four long ās in the second half of the word each get their full length; the word is largely made of them, and clipping any one of them makes it unrecognizable.

For archanā the three datives are janmamṛtyujarātaptajanaviśrāntidāyinyai, sarvopaniṣadudghuṣṭāyai and śāntyatītakalātmikāyai. The first is a mouthful even by the standards of this hymn, and in nāmāvalī recitation it is the point where a chanter either has the compound properly memorized or discovers that he does not.

What the verse asks is unusually plain. The first name identifies the person reciting it: someone scorched by birth, death and old age is not a category of unfortunate other people. It is a description of anyone who is going to die, which is to say of the reciter, and the name offers not a remedy for the heat but an end to the exertion of enduring it. Having said that, the verse immediately moves out of the language of comfort and into the vocabulary of the tattva ladder, and the juxtaposition is the lesson: the rest on offer is not rest as ordinarily understood, but the condition named at the top of a scale where even peace has been left behind.

crossReferences.deva: स तस्मिन्नेवाकाशे स्त्रियमाजगाम बहुशोभमानामुमां हैमवतीं तां होवाच किमेतद्यक्षमिति ॥
crossReferences.iast: sa tasminn evākāśe striyam ājagāma bahu śobhamānām umāṃ haimavatīṃ tāṃ hovāca kim etad yakṣam iti ||
crossReferences.translation: In that very space he came upon a woman of great splendour, Umā, daughter of the snow mountain. He said to her: what was that spirit?
crossReferences.relevance: This is the passage the tradition points to first when it claims that the Upaniṣads proclaim her. Indra, having failed to identify the power that humbled the gods, learns what it was only from a woman who appears where it had been; the disclosure of the absolute is placed in a female mouth in one of the oldest and least sectarian of the Upaniṣads. Whether or not this amounts to all the Upaniṣads shouting her name, it is the foothold from which the larger claim was built.

crossReferences.deva: न तस्य कार्यं करणं च विद्यते न तत्समश्चाभ्यधिकश्च दृश्यते । परास्य शक्तिर्विविधैव श्रूयते स्वाभाविकी ज्ञानबलक्रिया च ॥
crossReferences.iast: na tasya kāryaṃ karaṇaṃ ca vidyate na tatsamaś cābhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate | parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca ||
crossReferences.translation: He has neither work to do nor instrument to do it with; no one is seen equal to him or greater. His supreme power is heard of as manifold indeed, inherent to him, consisting of knowledge, strength and action.
crossReferences.relevance: The single most quoted Upaniṣadic sentence in later Śākta and Śaiva argument, because it says in an unimpeachably old text that the absolute has a power, that the power is manifold, and that it belongs to his own nature rather than being added from outside. Sarvopaniṣadudghuṣṭā rests on passages of this kind, and the verb śrūyate, is heard, is close in force to udghuṣṭā, is shouted.

crossReferences.source: Bhagavad Gītā, chapter 13 (the numbering shifts by one depending on whether Arjuna's opening question is counted)
crossReferences.translation: Keeping in view the wrong and the suffering in birth, death, old age and sickness.
crossReferences.relevance: Almost the same compound as the one that opens this verse, in the Gītā's catalogue of what constitutes knowledge, with sickness added to the three. The parallel shows that the sahasranāma is not coining a phrase but invoking a standard diagnosis, and the difference in what follows is the point: the Gītā prescribes keeping the four in view, while the hymn names someone who gives the people burnt by them somewhere to stop.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: For the Kena episode in a translation that does not smooth over how strange it is. Olivelle's notes are also the best short guide to what the word upaniṣad actually meant to the people who used it, which is the hinge of the second name in this verse.

references.title: Eight Upaniṣads, with the Commentary of Śaṅkarācārya
references.author: tr. Swāmī Gambhīrānanda (Advaita Ashrama, 2 vols.)
references.note: The place to read the classical derivation of the word upaniṣad and to watch Śaṅkara handle the Umā Haimavatī episode, which he must take seriously and cannot take as goddess worship. The tension in his commentary is more instructive than either the text or the tradition on its own.

references.title: Śaivism and the Tantric Traditions
references.author: Alexis Sanderson, in The World's Religions, ed. S. Sutherland et al. (Routledge, 1988)
references.note: Forty pages that map the whole Śaiva and Śākta landscape, including the tattva hierarchy and the phases used to divide it. If you want to know exactly what Śāntyatītā is the top of, this is the shortest reliable route to it.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma with Bhāskararāya's Commentary
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library and Research Centre)
references.note: Consult it here for the claim that all the Upaniṣads proclaim her, where the commentarial tradition assembles its scriptural warrant. Reading the list of passages actually adduced is the fastest way to see how a Śākta reading of the Vedānta is constructed.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma, sung by M. S. Subbulakshmi
references.author: widely reissued; originally recorded for HMV
references.note: The recording most South Indian households learned the hymn from, and the standard against which pace is judged. This verse is a good place to test any recording: a chanter who does not slow down for the sixteen-syllable name is treating it as filler, and Subbulakshmi does not.
